lesson.title: Electron Clouds: Where Quantum Mechanics Replaced the Solar System
lesson.summary: An atomic orbital is a three dimensional region of space where an electron is likely to be found, not a fixed path, and orbitals are the individual "rooms" that make up each subshell.
lesson.body:
Early models of the atom, especially the Bohr model, pictured electrons as tiny planets circling the nucleus in fixed circular paths at fixed distances. That picture explained the simple line spectrum of hydrogen well enough to be famous, but it fails for every atom with more than one electron, and it violates a deeper rule of quantum mechanics called the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: you cannot simultaneously know an electron's exact position and its exact momentum. If you cannot know exactly where an electron is, you cannot draw it a precise orbit. Quantum mechanics replaced the orbit with something less picturable but far more accurate.

That replacement is the orbital. An orbital is a three dimensional region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability, usually defined as about 90 percent, of finding a particular electron. Mathematically, an orbital comes from a wavefunction, a solution to the Schrodinger equation, and the square of that wavefunction gives the probability density at each point in space. Instead of a sharp line, you get a fuzzy cloud that is dense where the electron is likely to be and thin where it is not. Nobody claims the electron is smeared out physically; the cloud describes probability, not a blurred particle.

This is where subshells reappear. You already know that each shell (given by the principal quantum number n) splits into subshells labeled s, p, d, and f, and that these subshells differ in shape and energy. An orbital is the individual unit inside a subshell: the s subshell is built from exactly one orbital, the p subshell from three, the d subshell from five, and the f subshell from seven. The number of orbitals in a subshell follows the simple pattern 2l + 1, where l is the angular momentum quantum number (0 for s, 1 for p, 2 for d, 3 for f). Within one atom, all the orbitals in a given subshell have the same energy, so chemists call them degenerate.

Every orbital, no matter which subshell it belongs to, can hold a maximum of two electrons, and those two electrons must have opposite spins. That capacity limit is not arbitrary; it comes from the Pauli exclusion principle, which you will meet in detail soon. For now, picture the simplest case: hydrogen has one electron, and it occupies the 1s orbital, the lowest energy, most compact spherical region closest to the nucleus. Helium has two electrons, and both fit into that same 1s orbital, but only because their spins are opposite; two electrons with the same spin cannot share an orbital, full stop.

As atoms get larger, orbitals stack up in a predictable order of increasing energy: 1s, then 2s and 2p, then 3s and 3p, and so on, with a few sequence twists that show up once you reach the d subshells. That energy ordering is exactly what the Aufbau principle uses to predict how electrons fill a real atom, and the specific three dimensional shapes of s, p, d, and f orbitals, spheres, dumbbells, and more complex lobed forms, are what govern how atoms point their electron density toward each other when bonds form. Orbitals are the geometry underneath every electron configuration you will write from here on.
